own_scenes.desc: Entre 1972 y 1976 la comunidad negra cambió más que nunca, pero fuera de los telediarios: los líderes radicales, en los tribunales; la revolución, convertida en estilo; «Power to the people» en 1972 y «Have a nice day» en 1976. La cultura negra se volvió nacional: «hermano» y «hermana», el saludo de cinco, «Right on», afros, plataformas, dashikis, astrología y marihuana; Sly, Angela Davis o Tina Turner como embajadores del estilo y bailes nuevos (el robot, el penguin) extendidos por la televisión. Lo funky, palabrota en los sesenta, se volvió «baaad»: tras «Ain’t It Funky» y «Funky Drummer» llegaron el «Funky Chicken», el «Funky Worm», el «Funky Nassau» o «Funky Music Sho Nuff Turns Me On». La tele pasó de I Spy a The Flip Wilson Show y Sanford and Son, con el cómico guarro Redd Foxx. Soul Train, de Don Cornelius (exmarine y DJ de Chicago, financiado por Sears y Afro Sheen), fue la meca del decenio: la sexualidad negra sin diluir cada sábado por la mañana; Elton John fue el primer blanco en actuar. Los Dells cantaron «The Origin of Funk» («ahora que lo hemos recuperado») e Ishmael Reed imaginó en Mumbo Jumbo (1972) el «Jes Grew», una antiplaga rítmica negra que contagia a América, fuente de inspiración de Clinton. Era la transformación final: el amor propio total, ser funky y orgulloso.

refs.q: Funkiness was everywhere in the early seventies.
refs.para: Funkiness was everywhere in the early seventies. What was a bad word in the 1960s, all of a sudden was baaad! What began as an affinity for “gettin’ down” proliferated in black dance music in the 1970s. A series of dance singles using funky in the title hit the radio as the decade dawned. James Brown’s instrumental “Ain’t it Funky” in 1969 and “Funky Drummer” in 1970 paved the way. Within the next three years there was “Funky Chicken,” “Funky Penguin,” “Funky Granny,” “Funky Worm,” “Funky Nassau,” “The Funky Man,” and the Temptations’ “Funky Music Sho Nuff Turns Me On.” There were the dances—the funky chicken, the funky walk, the funky butt, and, as joked about on James Brown’s 1972 “Escapism,” the new dance “The Funky Train.” It had finally become cool to be funky.
refs.chapter: Cap. 13: Los funky setenta: Livin’ for the City

refs.q: Everyone got up on Saturday mornings to watch Soul Train, “the hippest trip in America,”
refs.para: The most undiluted showcase of black sexuality in the country was a black enterprise that continues to this day. Everyone got up on Saturday mornings to watch Soul Train, “the hippest trip in America,” the black answer to American Bandstand, and a cultural mecca for the entire decade of the seventies. The wild syncopated gyrations of the Soul Train dancers were an erotic-hypnotic revelation for most unfunky Americans. Always freshly dressed in the latest fashions, hitting the latest dances, and the right-on soul stars lip-syncing their soon-to-be classic hits made Soul Train essential seventies, despite the droll style of host Don Cornelius.

refs.q: Actually Jes Grew was an anti-plague.
refs.para: Actually Jes Grew was an anti-plague. Some plagues caused the body to waste away; Jes Grew enlivened the host. Other plagues were accompanied by bad air (malaria). Jes Grew victims said that the air was as clear as they had ever seen it and that there was the aroma of roses and perfumes which had never before enticed their nostrils. Some plagues arise from decomposing animals, but Jes Grew is electric as life and is characterized by ebullience and ecstasy. Terrible plagues were due to the wrath of God; but Jes Grew is the delight of the gods.
refs.chapter: Cap. 13: Los funky setenta: Livin’ for the City

refs.q: This was the final transformation that needed to take place: total self-love.
refs.para: With the ethereal nature of funk as part of the new black identity in the early seventies, the “Negro” to “black” transformation would come full circle. What was once something to be ashamed of—a sweaty, spirited, sexually expressive lifestyle—was now becoming something to take pride in. The Funk was not a curse, it was a blessing—and it was spreading around the world like a disease. This was the final transformation that needed to take place: total self-love.
